news.full_article_text: Danish minister visits India to advance green energy, trade partnership, maritime ties Lidegaard, who visited Mumbai and New Delhi during November 2-3, described India as an increasingly important partner for Denmark Moves by India and Denmark to take their unique Green Strategic Partnership into its next phase got a boost during Danish business minister Martin Lidegaard’s visit to the country that focused on strengthening cooperation in trade, innovation, green technologies and maritime affairs. Lidegaard, who visited Mumbai and New Delhi during November 2-3, described India as an increasingly important partner for Denmark, economically, technologically and geopolitically. Denmark has strong skills that can support India’s ambitions in areas such as renewable energy and AI, he said. The next phase of the bilateral Green Strategic Partnership, established in 2020, envisages enhanced cooperation in areas of shared economic and strategic interest. A new joint action plan and more high-level visits in support of the partnership are currently being prepared. “I am in India to learn about the speed and scale of your country’s transition, strengthen our partnership and open doors for Danish companies,” said Lidegaard, who began his visit on Monday in Mumbai, where he visited APM Terminals, operated by the Danish shipping company Maersk, and discussed new economic opportunities with Maharashtra Governor Jishnu Dev Varma. In New Delhi, Lidegaard met commerce minister Piyush Goyal to discuss growing trade and economic opportunities against the backdrop of the expanding bilateral partnership and the upcoming India-European Union (EU) free trade agreement. More than 200 Danish companies operating in India employ more than 100,000 people. He also met Union ports and shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal to discuss cooperation in green shipping, sustainable port development and green corridors. He also advanced the India-Denmark energy partnership while meeting Union renewable energy minister Pralhad Joshi and participating in the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo 2026. Discussions focused on expanding commercial opportunities and Denmark’s support for India’s transition to a more efficient, reliable and sustainable energy system. Denmark is the second-largest government contributor to the International Solar Alliance outside India. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Rezaul H Laskar Rezaul Hasan Laskar is Foreign Editor with the Hindustan Times, which he joined in 2015. He began as a journalist in his hometown of Shillong in northeast India and has worked in newspapers and wire services over the years. He moved to New Delhi in 1997 and initially focused on defence, national security, Jammu and Kashmir and the northeast, while also working of foreign policy and international relations. He has been part of the media delegation accompanying PMs on foreign visits and has reported from destinations ranging from Tibet to Ukraine. Between 2007 and 2013, he was the Press Trust of India correspondent in Pakistan, one of only two Indian journalists allowed to report from the country. He extensively covered Pakistan’s domestic politics and the life of the common people, as well as the fallout of the 2008 Mumbai attacks on India-Pakistan relations and the subsequent trial in Pakistan of the suspects involved in the attack. As part of his reportage in Pakistan, he travelled the breadth of the country, from the Swat Valley to Balochistan. Reza’s first gig in journalism was writing a weekly music column, and music – especially classic rock – remains a keen interest. He is also a movie buff and a keen photographer. Read More

news.headline: EC: Previously enrolled voters can submit form 6 for inclusion
news.story_lead: EC: Previously enrolled voters can submit form 6 for inclusion The Election Commission on Tuesday said previously enrolled voters can submit Form 6 for inclusion as electors if their names are missing from draft Special Intensive Revision (SIR) rolls. The clarification came days after the Supreme Court asked ECI not to make nearly 4.3 million Delhi residents – whose names were removed from the electoral rolls after they could not be found at their last known addresses – reapply as new voters through Form 6 provided they were on the 2026 rolls. Instead, it suggested that such voters be permitted to restore their names through Form 8, which is intended for address-related changes, or through the enumeration process.
news.full_article_text: EC: Previously enrolled voters can submit form 6 for inclusion The Election Commission on Tuesday said previously enrolled voters can submit Form 6 for inclusion as electors if their names are missing from draft Special Intensive Revision (SIR) rolls. The clarification came days after the Supreme Court asked ECI not to make nearly 4.3 million Delhi residents – whose names were removed from the electoral rolls after they could not be found at their last known addresses – reapply as new voters through Form 6 provided they were on the 2026 rolls. Instead, it suggested that such voters be permitted to restore their names through Form 8, which is intended for address-related changes, or through the enumeration process. In a letter to all state chief electoral officers, ECI said that it was brought to its notice that certain people whose names did not figure in the draft electoral roll published during the ongoing SIR were hesitant to submit Form 6 as they were also required to furnish a declaration to the effect that their name was being included in the electoral rolls for the first time. “Therefore, such electors believe that submission of Form 6, in view of their previous enrolment, would amount to making a false declaration and render them liable for prosecution under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950,” it said. ECI clarified that voters whose names did not figure in the draft SIR rolls could submit Form 6 to seek fresh inclusion in the final voters’ list, even if they were enrolled previously. Citing a Delhi high court’s October 14 judgment, ECI said the apprehension of making a false declaration was misplaced. A senior official in the Delhi CEO’s office said the machinery on the ground had received no guidance on the Form8 route. “We haven’t received any SOPs or instructions from the ECI to get people placed under ASDD categories to fill Form8,” the official said. Activists Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri also wrote to ECI and Delhi CEO, seeking “immediate compliance”.

news.headline: Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
news.story_lead: - Published 3 November 2026, 03:32 GMT The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count. The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state. Two lower courts had already rejected the request.
news.full_article_text: - Published 3 November 2026, 03:32 GMT The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count. The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state. Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate. The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term. The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction. "The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads. Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots. California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office. - What are the US midterms? A simple guide Published 9 hours ago The justice department sent letters to the California secretary of state and Los Angeles County Registrar last month, demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration "believe" are "likely" non-citizens, according to court documents. About a week later, armed officials from the Department of Homeland Security delivered letters to county officials and employees across California threatening criminal charges if they didn't sequester those ballots. In a 22-page brief reviewed by the BBC, the justice department maintained that ballots cast by non-citizens could "debase or dilute valid votes". On Friday, a federal appeals court declined the government's request to segregate the ballots. California election officials have questioned the accuracy of the government's claims, and have said the list of names the government has provided is riddled with inaccuracies. They have expressed concern that eligible voters could be disenfranchised and said segregating ballots whilst voting is underway is unfeasible. What are Americans voting for this election? The attempts are a part of a years-long campaign by Trump and his administration to fight alleged voter fraud that they believe is widespread, despite research showing that it is extremely rare. President Trump has repeatedly claimed that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally, and he blames much of it on the so-called "mail-in" or postal voting that is permitted in many Democratic states. Last week in a scathing ruling, district judge David Carter said the government's move in California was indicative of an "ongoing pattern of attempted election interference" on the part of the Trump administration. The judge added that "never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch". With additional reporting by the BBC's David Willis Related topics - US midterm elections 2026 - Voting rights in the United States More on this story - Judge orders Trump administration to stop threatening US election officials Published 2 days ago

news.full_article_text: Evening News Brief November 3: Supreme Court says no group can occupy protest site indefinitely, US votes in midterm elections Key developments included the Supreme Court’s remarks on protest-site occupations and US elections that will determine control of Congress. Good evening, readers. From the Supreme Court's remarks on indefinite protests to the high-stakes US midterm elections, several key developments made headlines today. Here are the key stories of the day. No individual, group can occupy a designated protest site indefinitely: Supreme Court The Supreme Court on Tuesday said no individual, group or organisation could claim an indefinite right to occupy a designated protest site, underlining that others too have an equal constitutional right to use the same public space to raise their grievances. The observations came as the court heard a clutch of petitions arising from the police action during the July protests led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), including allegations of mass detentions, police excesses, internet restrictions and the closure of metro stations. Read more. US midterm elections 2026: Polls open in several US states as Democrats seek control of both chambers of Congress Deep Dive Voters across several US states are heading to polling stations, joining millions who have already cast their ballots ahead of Election Day. Polling stations have opened in some East Coast states, including Connecticut, Maine, New York and New Jersey, as well as parts of Kentucky and Indiana. Voters will decide which party controls the US House of Representatives and the Senate. Democrats need to win four additional Senate seats and three House seats to take control of both chambers from Republicans. The Senate races in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas are among the key contests to watch. House battlegrounds are spread across the country. Track live updates here. Dia Mirza's Diwali video removal unfortunate, contrary to secular spirit: Bombay high court The removal of actor Dia Mirza’s video for the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC)'s eco-friendly Diwali campaign was “very unfortunate” and contrary to the “secular spirit” of the country, the Bombay high court said on Tuesday. The court’s remarks came amid a massive row in the state, after the civic body selectively removed the actor’s clip from social media following objections from a Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader and mayor Ritu Tawde's comments labelling her as "anti-Hindu". Mirza, however, said efforts to reduce air pollution should be welcomed as it is a matter of public health. Read more. Ranbir Kapoor says he doen't like the term ‘Bollywood’ as it derives from Hollywood Actor Ranbir Kapoor has made his stance clear on the use of the term ‘Bollywood’ to describe Hindi cinema, or sometimes all of Indian cinema. In an interview with a British media outlet, Ranbir agreed he was not a fan of the term and would prefer to be known as an Indian actor rather than a Bollywood star. Ranbir is promoting his upcoming film, Ramayana, for which he was recently in London along with castmates Sai Pallavi and Yash. There, the actor spoke to ITV where the host asked him why he was not a fan of the ‘umbrella term Bollywood’ used to describe Indian films. Ranbir responded, “I think it's just a term used as a derivative of Hollywood. Because it was Bombay at that time, so it became Bollywood, and the Telugu industry became Tollywood, and they had all these different-sounding names.” Read more. Badminton fund row: SAI, BAI administrative tussle left players to fend for themselves Administrative delays reportedly led to the Sports Authority of India (SAI) not approving funds for the participation of top Indian badminton players, led by PV Sindhu and Lakshya Sen, in the recent European swing of tournaments which ended with both the India No.1 players crowned champions at the Hylo Open in Staarbrucken, Germany on Sunday. The issue has sparked a controversy over players being left to organise their own finances for the trip that involved tournaments in four countries — Finland, Denmark, France and Germany. However, it is learnt that the Badminton Association of India (BAI) did not receive Sports Authority of India's (SAI) clearance in time because it delayed sending the list of tournaments for approval. The Union home ministry on Tuesday appointed 1995-batch IPS officer Rajesh Kumar as the new director general of police (DGP) of Arunachal Pradesh, a day after he was prematurely repatriated from the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) to his parent cadre. The appointments committee of the Cabinet on Monday cleared the Union home ministry’s proposal to repatriate Kumar prematurely to his parent AGMUT cadre with “immediate effect” from the CRPF, where he was serving as Special DG. In an order issued on Wednesday, the home ministry posted Kumar as the new DGP of the border state, succeeding the incumbent and his batchmate, Shiv Darshan Singh Jamwal, who has been transferred to Delhi. The change comes at a time when a section of the tribal community in Arunachal Pradesh has been protesting against the proposed 11,200-megawatt multipurpose hydroelectric project on the Siang River, considered one of India’s largest. The project, envisioned as one of India’s largest hydropower initiatives, has faced sustained opposition from sections of the indigenous Adi community, particularly residents of the proposed project-affected areas. Also Read: ‘Disagreement is your right, not talking about dam construction now’: CM Pema Khandu amid protests against Siang project The opposition stems primarily from apprehensions over the submergence of ancestral villages, displacement, loss of agricultural land and forests, and the possible disruption of the community’s traditional way of life. The project has also assumed strategic significance for the Centre, which views it as important in the context of China’s proposed massive hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo River in Tibet, which enters India as the Siang. On Monday, Arunachal chief minister Pema Kandu had said in a statement that no decision has been taken without consent on construction of the dam will while appealing to protests to withdraw their 36-hour shutdown call in Upper Siang region. “Let me be clear. We are not talking about dam construction at this stage,” Khandu said , explaining that the government was considering only a Pre-Feasibility Report (PFR) to assess the project’s viability and potential implications.

* **Judicial Action:** The court paused the official remuneration of the municipal head to enforce institutional accountability regarding urban local governance and public land management.
